kjv.text: Who hath saved us, and called us with an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began,

bsb.text: He has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began.

teacher.name: Matthew Henry
teacher.label: Henry treats verse 9 together with verses 9-10

flow.text: Henry shows what great things God has done for us through the gospel, giving Timothy reasons to suffer for it.

Observe, The gospel aims at our salvation: *He has saved us,* and we must not think much to suffer for that which we hope to be saved by. He has begun to save us, and will complete it in due time; for God calls those things that are not (that are not yet completed) as though they were (Ro 4:17); therefore he says, who *has* saved us.
God has begun saving us and will finish the work, so we should not hesitate to suffer for the salvation we hope to receive.

It is designed for our sanctification: *And called us with a holy calling,* called us to holiness. Christianity is a calling, a holy calling; it is the calling wherewith we are called, the calling to which we are called, to labour in it.
The gospel calls us to holiness, and wherever that call truly takes hold, it makes people holy.

The origin of it is the free grace and eternal purpose of God in Christ Jesus. If we had merited it, it had been hard to suffer for it; but our salvation by it is of free grace, and not according to our works, and therefore we must not think much to suffer for it.
Our salvation comes from God's free grace and eternal purpose, not from anything we have earned, so suffering for it is reasonable.

By the gospel of Christ death is abolished: *He has abolished death,* not only weakened it, but taken it out of the way, has broken the power of death over us; by taking away sin he has abolished death (for the sting of death is sin, 1Co 15:56), in altering the property of it, and breaking the power of it.
Through the gospel, Christ has broken death's power over believers, turning it from an enemy into a passage to peace.

He has *brought life and immortality to light by the gospel;* he has shown us another world more clearly than it was before discovered under any former dispensation, and the happiness of that world, the certain recompence of our obedience by faith: we all with open face, as in a glass, behold the glory of God. He has brought it to light, not only set it before us, but offered it to us, by the gospel.

morning.say: Carry with you today what the gospel reveals: life and immortality are now brought to light for all who believe.

flags.issue: The verse (2 Timothy 1:9) does not mention death or its abolishment. This connecting sentence introduces content from 2 Timothy 1:10 (not provided in the verse), shifting beyond the stated verse's scope.
